docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, a key component of being skilled that distinguishes skills from habits, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Skills require control over initiating the task, whereas habits are merely triggered by environmental cues.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text: According to Ferdman (2026), agential control is essential because: - It allows flexible links between thought and action that evolve even after expertise - It enables agents to initiate activities rather than merely responding to triggers - It's necessary for developing "the arts of personhood" - capacities constituting human flourishing

docs.title: Contrast with Habitual Behavior
docs.text:
Critical distinction between skills and habits: - Skills: Require control over initiating the activity; agent has full control over starting - Habits: Triggered by environment; agent performs in response to the trigger

An agent performing out of habit, responding to environmental triggers, is less skilled than one who initiated the activity with full agential control.

docs.title: Implications for AI Systems
docs.text:
AI risks undermining agential control by: - Automating routine tasks that provide habituation opportunities - Creating environments where users respond to AI recommendations rather than initiating plans - Encouraging "plan-following" behavior over "plan-forming"

This is particularly concerning for artificial-personal-assistants, which may encourage dependency on AI-generated plans rather than developing life-planning capacity.

docs.title: Importance for Market Research
docs.text: Agential control is crucial because it: - Enables researchers to adjust methodologies in response to unexpected findings - Allows critical evaluation of AI-generated insights rather than uncritical acceptance - Supports development of practical wisdom (phronesis) in research design - Preserves ability to initiate novel research approaches rather than following patterns

docs.title: Plan-Forming vs Plan-Following
docs.text:
Ferdman distinguishes: - Plan-forming: Requires exercising epistemic, moral, social and creative capacities; involves self-deliberation, settling functions, and coordination - Plan-following: More like habit triggered by environmental cues; lacks responsibility for plan failure

When AI offloads planning, it reduces opportunities to develop practical wisdom - "knowing effective means to ends with accurate situational understanding."

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: AI Adoption Intensity Terciles is a methodology developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to categorize firms based on the intensity of their AI adoption, measured by the PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. Firms are classified as AI adopters when they have three consecutive months of at least $100 in AI vendor spending
  2. Adoption intensity is measured as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over the first three months after adoption
  3. Among treated firms, PEPM values are sorted and divided into three equal groups (terciles):
  4. High intensity: top tercile (most intensive AI adopters)
  5. Medium intensity: middle tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom tercile (least intensive AI adopters)
  7. For analysis, firms are often grouped as:
  8. High intensity: top tercile
  9. Low intensity: bottom two terciles combined

docs.title: Rationale for Tercile Approach
docs.text:
• Allows researchers to examine differential impacts of AI adoption based on intensity
  • Reveals that not all AI adopters experience the same employment effects
  • Helps address selection bias by comparing firms with similar eventual adoption intensity
  • Shows that substantial employment gains are concentrated among high-intensity adopters

docs.title: Key Findings Using Intensity Terciles
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters grew total employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • High-intensity gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months, suggesting a learning curve
  • Employment gains were broad across roles for high-intensity adopters (engineering, sales, administration, customer service)

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: This methodology revealed a critical insight often missed in prior research: AI's labor market effects differ substantially based on adoption intensity. Studies that treat all adopters the same may miss these nuanced patterns.

docs.text: Methodological advances in measuring AI adoption, particularly the shift from occupational exposure scores to direct firm-level spending data. The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study represents a breakthrough in this area by using observed AI vendor payments rather than theoretical exposure metrics.

docs.title: Ramp-Revelio Methodology
docs.text:
The study introduces the AI Spend Per Employee Methodology (PEPM):

  1. Adoption definition: Three consecutive months of ≥$100 AI vendor spend
  2. Intensity measure: PEPM = (sum of first 3 months' AI spend) / (3 × baseline headcount)
  3. Intensity stratification: Low (bottom two PEPM terciles), High (top PEPM tercile)
  4. Comparison design: Later adopters within same intensity group

This approach overcomes four critical limitations of prior methods:

  1. Direct observation: Measures actual adoption behavior rather than theoretical exposure
  2. Timing precision: Captures exact adoption month rather than imputed timing
  3. Intensity dimension: Reveals differential effects by adoption intensity
  4. Firm-level specificity: Avoids occupational aggregation that masks firm differences

docs.title: Observed Spending Threshold
docs.text: The $100/month threshold excludes one-off experiments while capturing sustained adoption, addressing the "Is this really AI adoption?" question that plagues survey-based approaches.

docs.title: PEPM Metric
docs.text: Using baseline headcount in the denominator makes intensity comparable across firm sizes and keeps employee scale predetermined relative to adoption timing.

docs.title: Staggered Treatment Design
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework accounts for heterogeneous treatment timing, avoiding biases in traditional event-study approaches.

docs.title: Evidence of Impact
docs.text: This methodological innovation revealed findings invisible to exposure-based studies: - Only high-intensity adopters (+10.2% headcount growth) showed significant employment effects - Entry-level roles grew 12.0% among high-intensity adopters, contradicting exposure-based predictions - Effects concentrated in Information sector (+13.4% growth), not uniformly distributed

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological shift has critical implications:

  • Vendor evaluation: Must measure actual usage intensity, not just adoption status
  • Impact assessment: Requires tracking spending patterns over time, not binary adoption
  • Benchmarking: Industry comparisons must account for intensity differences
  • ROI calculation: Benefits appear only above critical intensity thresholds

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This innovation directly addresses the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and explains the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies observed across research. It represents a critical advance over the pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index used in pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer.

docs.title: Practical Implementation
docs.text:
For market research organizations, adopting this methodological innovation means: - Tracking actual AI spending rather than adoption claims - Measuring intensity through normalized spending metrics - Comparing against firms with similar pre-adoption characteristics - Focusing on sustained usage patterns rather than initial adoption

Without these methodological improvements, organizations risk misattributing effects or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns—precisely what the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study demonstrates.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. As rigorously documented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, these selection effects mean AI adopters were already distinct from non-adopters before AI adoption, creating significant methodological challenges.

docs.title: Key Evidence
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study demonstrates dramatic pre-adoption differences:

Characteristic AI Adopters Never Adopters Difference Headcount (mean) 144.2 103.9 +40.3* Engineering share 26.8% 18.6% +8.2* Entry-level share 42.1% 50.4% -8.3* YoY growth (median) 6.0% 1.6% +4.4* Mean salary $110,346 $93,847 +$16,499* Tech-adjacent sector 54.2% 25.9% +28.3* VC-backed 34.0% 9.5% +24.5*

*Statistically significant at p<0.01

docs.title: Methodological Implications
docs.text:
This selection bias creates three critical challenges for AI impact research:

  1. Confounded comparisons: Simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons conflate AI effects with pre-existing differences
  2. Pre-trend divergence: Adopters were already on different growth trajectories before adoption (see Figure 4 in Ramp-Revelio study)
  3. Sector concentration: AI adoption heavily concentrated in Information (53.7%), Finance (43.6%), and Professional Services (36.0%)

docs.title: Addressing the Bias
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study employs sophisticated methods to address selection bias:

  • Preferred comparison: Later adopters within the same eventual intensity group
  • Sector fixed effects: Controlling for industry composition differences
  • Event-time analysis: Tracking pre-treatment parallel trends
  • Intensity stratification: Separating low vs. high adoption intensity effects

This approach revealed that only high-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no significant change.

docs.title: Contrast with Exposure-Based Studies
docs.text: This selection bias explains why exposure-based studies (like pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer) often produce different findings than spending-based studies: - Exposure scores cannot distinguish firms that adopt AI from those that don't - They assume uniform adoption effects across firms with identical workforce composition - They miss the critical intensity dimension revealed by actual spending data

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This concept has profound implications for insights organizations:

  • Vendor selection: AI tools adopted by leading firms may reflect pre-existing advantages rather than causal benefits
  • Implementation strategy: Success depends on organizational readiness, not just tool adoption
  • Impact measurement: Must account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI initiatives
  • Benchmarking: Comparing against industry averages without controlling for selection effects is misleading

docs.text: This concept is central to understanding the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies problem and represents a key ai-adoption-methodological-innovation addressed by the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study. It explains why the employment gains documented in that study are concentrated among high-intensity adopters in specific sectors, rather than across all AI adopters.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, addressing selection bias requires: - Never comparing AI adopters to non-adopters without controlling for pre-existing differences - Measuring adoption intensity (PEPM) rather than binary adoption status - Using staggered adoption timing in evaluation designs - Focusing on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact

Without these precautions, organizations risk attributing pre-existing advantages to AI adoption or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns.

docs.title: Ai democratization
docs.text: AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI democratization describes how artificial intelligence makes advanced capabilities accessible by automating complex expert tasks, thereby reducing expertise requirements for certain occupations. As quantified in Figure 2 of the PwC 2026 report, this process affects 52% of global job postings. Concrete examples include [[recruiters]] (AI automates CV screening while humans handle contract negotiation) and [[inventory-clerks]] (AI manages stock optimization while humans perform physical movement). Figure 3 demonstrates democratization is particularly strong in high AI exposure jobs, where expertise requirements decrease significantly. Crucially, Figure 11 reveals that despite reduced expertise demands, democratized roles maintain high epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability, or interpersonal skills. The report warns that while democratization expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform data analysis), it may compress career ladders and reduce skill development opportunities without targeted interventions. This concept represents one of two primary pathways (alongside ai-professionalization) in AI's labor market restructuring. Organizations can leverage democratization through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Supply and Demand' dimension, redesigning roles to balance AI efficiency with human execution. The trend is accelerating post-2022, as shown in Figure 9's widening skill transformation gap, requiring proactive workforce planning to ensure equitable access to emerging opportunities in democratized roles.

docs.title: AI Deskilling as a Structural Problem
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-19

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. This should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions, not merely an individual responsibility issue.

docs.title: Key Insights
docs.text:
Ferdman's (2026) analysis in AI & Society fundamentally shifts the deskilling discourse by:

  1. Moving beyond individual responsibility narratives that expect people to "will themselves to cultivate 'the arts of personhood'"
  2. Introducing the concepts of capacity-hostile environments and capacity-conducive environments
  3. Demonstrating how AI's influence creates systemic conditions that inhibit capacity development
  4. Framing deskilling as a structural problem requiring societal solutions

docs.title: Structural Framework
docs.text:
The structural perspective on AI deskilling involves:

Individual Responsibility View Structural Perspective Focuses on how agents should engage with AI Examines what socio-technical environments best cultivate personhood Expects individuals to resist deskilling Recognizes environments shape capacity development Blames individuals for capacity loss Identifies systemic conditions creating capacity-hostile environments Treats deskilling as personal failure Understands deskilling as structural problem

docs.title: Core Human Capacities at Risk
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies four core human capacities threatened by AI-induced deskilling:

  1. Epistemic capacities: Theoretical and practical rationality necessary for knowledge and decision-making
  2. Social capacities: Moral and relational capacities for meaningful relationships
  3. Creative capacities: Ability to generate novel ideas and transform conceptual spaces
  4. Volitional capacity: Meta-capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, and grow

docs.title: Mechanisms of Structural Deskilling
docs.text:
AI creates capacity-hostile environments through:

  1. Narrowing the field of affordances - reducing action possibilities for capacity development
  2. Undermining embodied interaction - limiting opportunities for intersubjective habituation
  3. Encouraging plan-following - replacing plan-forming activities that develop practical wisdom
  4. Devaluing capacities - when persons develop capacities shallowly, they cannot learn to value mastery

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
This structural perspective explains the human-operating-model-gap - the growing disparity between AI capabilities and human systems. In market research, it manifests as:

  • The entry-level squeeze where foundational research tasks are automated
  • Declining development of epistemic capacities as researchers rely on AI summaries
  • Erosion of social capacities as client interactions become more mediated
  • Weakening of creative capacities as research design becomes standardized

docs.title: Societal Solutions
docs.text:
Rather than expecting researchers to be "virtuous superheroes," the structural perspective calls for: - Designing capacity-conducive research environments - Creating opportunities for embodied client interactions - Preserving space for plan-forming activities in research design - Developing mentorship structures that support intersubjective habituation

As Ferdman concludes: "Ultimately, it calls for a critical reflection on the values inherent in AI socio-technical systems and emphasizes the societal obligation to foster capacity-conducive environments in the age of AI."

docs.title: Ai job future framework
docs.text: A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The AI Job Future Framework, introduced in Figure 6 of PwC's 2026 report, provides a structured methodology to assess AI's occupational impact through four critical questions: (1) Expertise: How is AI changing required human expertise? (e.g., democratization reduces expertise needs while professionalization increases them); (2) Supply and Demand: How might job demand and worker supply shift as AI reshapes roles?; (3) AI's limitations: Where is human oversight needed for quality control or atypical cases?; and (4) Environmental forces: How do regulations, business bottlenecks, or ethics constrain AI adoption? The report demonstrates the framework's application across diverse occupations: For [[pharmacists]], AI handles prescription processing (Expertise shift) but humans manage patient counseling (AI's limitations); for [[software-developers]], AI generates code but humans focus on architecture (Environmental forces). Figure 9 validates the framework by showing how high AI exposure roles undergo 2.2x faster skill changes, directly addressing the Supply and Demand dimension. Organizations using this tool can anticipate skill shifts, redesign roles, and develop targeted training—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' (Figure 12). The framework also explains wage dynamics: roles requiring human oversight of AI (Question 3) command higher premiums, as seen in Figure 15's 62% average AI skill premium. By systematically addressing these questions, employers can transform AI disruption into opportunity, while workers identify future-proof career paths in the evolving labor market. This methodology has become essential for strategic workforce planning in the AI era.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Capacity-conducive environments are environments that actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these environments provide structured and unstructured embodied interactions necessary for intersubjective habituation of capacities, serving as alternatives to capacity-hostile conditions.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, capacity-conducive environments have several key characteristics:

  1. Rich Affordance Space: They provide abundant action possibilities that trigger and support the development of multiple human capacities simultaneously.

  2. Embodied Interaction: They encourage physical presence and sensory experience in skill development, particularly critical for social and moral capacities.

  3. Intersubjective Learning: They facilitate mentor-mentee relationships and shared understanding about both the mechanical aspects of skills and their intrinsic value.

  4. Agential Control Development: They afford opportunities for users to initiate activities and adjust their execution, rather than merely responding to environmental triggers.

  5. Volitional Capacity Support: They encourage the development of willpower by presenting appropriately challenging activities that require effort and perseverance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Community Centers: Provide spaces for structured and unstructured embodied interactions that foster shared experiences necessary for social capacity development.

  2. Public Libraries: Afford opportunities for reading, research, and community engagement that trigger epistemic and social capacities.

  3. Quality Public Spaces: Encourage spontaneous social interactions and civic engagement that develop moral and relational capacities.

  4. Apprenticeship Models: Create environments where novices learn from mentors through embodied practice, shared valuing, and gradual habituation of skills.

  5. Collaborative Research Environments: In market research settings, teams that engage in co-creation with clients and participants, rather than relying solely on AI tools, create capacity-conducive environments for developing critical thinking and creativity.

docs.title: Contrast with Capacity-Hostile Environments
docs.text: Unlike capacity-hostile-environments, which restrict opportunities for capacity development through narrow fields of affordances, capacity-conducive environments actively encourage the cultivation of human capacities. Crucially, they don't merely provide opportunities for capacity exercise but actively encourage such exercise, recognizing that "merely having the opportunity to φ does not guarantee that the agent will actually φ and engage the capacities involved in φ-ing."

docs.title: Implementation in Organizations
docs.text: Ferdman suggests that organizations can foster capacity-conducive environments by: - Creating public goods like community centers and quality public spaces - Designing workspaces that encourage embodied interaction - Implementing mentorship programs that emphasize both skill mechanics and value - Avoiding indiscriminate automation of routine tasks that deprive users of habituation opportunities - Evaluating AI applications based on their conduciveness to capacity cultivation

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In the market research industry, capacity-conducive environments would: - Encourage researchers to engage directly with research participants - Support embodied interactions that develop empathy and social understanding - Create opportunities for mentorship in research design and interpretation - Balance AI tool usage with human judgment development - Foster environments where researchers can develop practical wisdom through real-world experience

Organizations should evaluate their AI adoption strategies based on whether they create capacity-conducive or capacity-hostile environments for their researchers, as outlined in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.text: Capacity-hostile environments restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for the development and exercise of core human capacities, as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. These environments afford opportunities for shallow skilling while restricting fuller development of capacities, with significant implications for AI's impact on human flourishing.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text: According to Ferdman (2026), capacity-hostile environments: - Restrict, limit, or narrow the field of affordances for capacity development - Afford opportunities for shallow skilling in capacities - Restrict opportunities for well-rounded development and exercise of capacities - Undermine the process of capacity cultivation through habituation - May encourage plan-following rather than plan-forming behavior

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text: In market research, capacity-hostile environments might include: - AI tools automating entire research processes without preserving critical thinking opportunities - Systems replacing human judgment in data interpretation without feedback mechanisms - Workflows minimizing embodied, intersubjective interactions necessary for social capacities - Platforms encouraging researchers to become "plan-followers" rather than "plan-formers"

docs.title: Structural Mechanisms
docs.text: Ferdman identifies key mechanisms through which AI creates capacity-hostile environments: 1. Automation of routine tasks: Deprives users of "cognitive musculature" strengthening through routine opportunities (Lee et al. 2025) 2. Reduced embodied interaction: Limits opportunities for recognizing others as moral agents through voice and gaze 3. Diminished intersubjectivity: Reduces shared valuing of capacities through mentor-mentee relationships 4. Affordance shrinkage: Systematic, enduring reduction in action possibilities that discourages compensation

docs.title: Contrast with Capacity-Conducive Environments
docs.text: Unlike capacity-conducive-environments, which actively encourage capacity development through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing, capacity-hostile environments systematically undermine cultivation conditions. Public goods like community centers, quality public spaces, and libraries encourage structured and unstructured embodied interactions necessary for capacity development.

docs.title: Structural Implications
docs.text: Ferdman argues capacity-hostile environments should be understood as structural problems requiring societal solutions. We cannot expect agents to be "virtuous superheroes" resisting deskilling if their environment doesn't value full maturation of human capacities. First, agents lack proper mentoring for "know-how," and second, they don't obtain shared understanding of capacity value.

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-18 Last Updated: 2026-07-19

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces, which enable innovation and adaptation. These capacities are constitutive of human flourishing and essential for responding to novel situations.

docs.title: Philosophical Framework
docs.text:
Based on Ferdman's (2026) analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, creative capacities involve:

  • Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Transforming conceptual spaces without relying merely on luck, accidents, or mechanical procedures
  • Generating novel insights and approaches
  • Adapting to unexpected events and surprises

As Ferdman explains: "The capacity for creativity involves making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas, transforming a conceptual space (Boden 2004), without relying merely on luck, accidents, or mechanical procedures (Gaut, 2010)."

docs.title: Role in Life-Planning and Execution
docs.text: Creative capacities are essential for effective life-planning because: - Planning is always incomplete and requires adaptation - Executing plans requires the ability to reconsider and respond to novel situations - Surprises and unexpected events demand creative problem-solving - Transforming conceptual spaces enables new approaches to challenges

docs.title: AI Threats to Creative Capacities
docs.text:
While AI systems can generate novel combinations, they threaten human creative capacities through:

  1. Reduced opportunities for creative habituation:
  2. "Automating routine tasks... deprives the user of the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature"

  3. Narrowing the field of affordances for creative exploration

  4. Encouraging plan-following over plan-forming:

  5. When AI provides ready-made solutions, users miss opportunities to develop creative problem-solving skills

  6. Reduced need to "reconsider and respond to novel situations, surprises and unexpected events"

  7. Superficial engagement with creativity:

  8. AI-generated suggestions may satisfy surface-level creative needs without developing deeper creative capacities
  9. Reduced motivation to engage in the difficult process of creative habituation

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
Creative capacities are fundamental to innovative market research:

  • Research design requires novel approaches to complex questions
  • Methodology development demands adaptation to unique research challenges
  • Insight generation involves making unfamiliar connections between data points
  • Problem-solving requires responding to unexpected research obstacles

The increasing use of AI in research threatens these capacities through: - Standardized AI-driven research templates replacing innovative design - Automated analysis diminishing opportunities for creative interpretation - Reduced need for researchers to develop novel approaches to challenges - Narrowing of the field of affordances for creative exploration

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
To maintain creative capacities in AI-augmented research environments: - Preserve space for human-led research design alongside AI suggestions - Create structured opportunities for researchers to develop novel methodologies - Design workflows that require researchers to explain why AI-generated insights are or aren't creative - Maintain embodied brainstorming sessions that support intersubjective creative development

As Ferdman (2026) notes regarding life-planning: "Planning one's life also involves the capacity for creativity, insofar as planning is always incomplete, and executing the plan requires the ability to reconsider and respond to novel situations, surprises and unexpected events." The same principle applies to research planning and execution, where creative capacities enable researchers to navigate the unexpected and generate truly innovative insights.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Developmental Perfectionism is a neo-Aristotelian approach to human flourishing where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life, providing the philosophical foundation for understanding why capacity-deskilling is harmful as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, Developmental Perfectionism has several critical features:

  1. Complex Unity: Human flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life rather than the maximization of isolated goods.

  2. Intrinsic Value: Humans exercise their capacities in activities that yield outcomes with intrinsic value like knowledge, beauty, morality, and friendship.

  3. Constitutive Relationship: The competent exercise of human capacities is the manifestation of the achievement of intrinsically valuable goods, making the capacities intrinsically valuable too.

  4. Developmental Process: Flourishing involves a developmental process where capacities are cultivated and exercised over time.

docs.title: Core Human Capacities
docs.text:
Developmental Perfectionism identifies several core human capacities that constitute flourishing:

  1. Epistemic Capacities: Include theoretical rationality (thinking, considering reasons to believe) and practical rationality (phronesis or practical wisdom).

  2. Social Capacities: Include the moral capacity as well as social and caring capacities for developing meaningful relationships of friendship and love.

  3. Creative Capacities: Involve making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas, transforming conceptual spaces without relying merely on luck or mechanical procedures.

  4. Volitional Capacity: The ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow to achieve intrinsically valuable goals. This is treated as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities.

docs.title: Why Deskilling is Harmful
docs.text:
Developmental Perfectionism provides the philosophical foundation for understanding why capacity-deskilling is harmful:

  1. Constitutive Relationship: "Capacity-deskilling is bad because our human capacities are constitutive of our flourishing. Impoverished capacities (i.e., capacity-deskilling), therefore, lead to impoverished lives."

  2. Value of Process: The value of achievements is gained from the competent exercise of capacities involved, not merely from the outcome (e.g., the value of being on Mt. Everest comes from the climb, not from simply being there).

  3. Holistic Nature: Human capacities rarely operate in isolation; they typically involve the exercise of multiple capacities simultaneously.

docs.title: Contrast with Skill Obsolescence
docs.text:
Developmental Perfectionism distinguishes between innocuous skill obsolescence and harmful capacity-deskilling:

  • Skill Obsolescence: "Skill obsolescence has always been part of human history, where technological developments free up time and resources for the cultivation of other skills." Deskilling of activities like hunting or basket-weaving may be innocuous.

  • Capacity-Deskilling: "The deskilling of our core human capacities—to know, create, form meaningful relationships, and use our willpower—is a different matter." Capacity-deskilling should always be a cause for worry.

docs.title: Implications for AI Ethics
docs.text:
Developmental Perfectionism provides a framework for evaluating AI systems:

  1. Structural Evaluation: Rather than focusing only on individual responsibility, we should evaluate what kind of socio-technical environments would be best for the cultivation of our personhood.

  2. Capacity-Conducive Design: AI systems should be designed to create environments conducive to capacity cultivation rather than hostile to it.

  3. Societal Obligation: There is a societal obligation to foster capacity-conducive environments in the age of AI, recognizing that deskilling is a structural problem requiring societal solutions.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In the market research industry, Developmental Perfectionism suggests that: - AI tools should be evaluated based on their impact on researchers' core human capacities - Organizations have an obligation to create research environments that foster capacity development - The value of market research lies not just in the outputs but in the competent exercise of capacities involved in the research process

Organizations should evaluate AI implementations based on whether they support or undermine the cultivation of researchers' human capacities, as outlined in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.text:
According to Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, embodiment in skilling has several critical features:

  1. Participatory Sense-Making: Embodied 'participatory sense-making' is constitutive of social cognition, for example in paying moral attention to others.

  2. Embodied Understanding: One comes to apprehend other perceived bodies as being similar loci of embodied subjectivity, creating 'embodied understanding.'

  3. Spontaneous Recognition: The spontaneity of recognizing others as moral agents is inherent in embodied interaction, whereas disembodied interaction requires more mental effort in attributing moral agency.

  4. Shared History Creation: Being embodied is critical for becoming skilled insofar as the process of 'shared valuing' of the skill requires some degree of doing something with the mentor(s), creating a shared history.

docs.title: Role in Capacity Development
docs.text:
Embodiment is fundamental to human capacity development:

  1. Moral Attention: The process of habituation of moral attention requires perceiving others as embodied beings through their voice and gaze.

  2. Meaningful Relationships: For the good of friendship, disembodied interactions make it harder to form meaningful relationships because "technologically mediated virtue friendships require more discipline for a diminished experience."

  3. Social Interaction Dynamics: "Meaning is generated and transformed in the interplay between the unfolding interaction process and the individuals engaged in it."

  4. Capacity Triggering: Environments that afford embodied interaction trigger the development of capacities that would otherwise remain dormant.

docs.title: Impact of AI on Embodiment
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine embodiment in several ways:

  1. Disembodied Interfaces: Digital interfaces that replace face-to-face interaction limit opportunities for embodied sense-making necessary for social and moral capacities.

  2. Reduced Shared Experiences: AI mediation decreases opportunities for creating the shared history and participatory sense-making regarding both the product of the skill and the skill itself.

  3. Automation of Physical Tasks: When AI handles tasks that would normally involve physical engagement, it deprives users of embodied learning opportunities.

  4. Fractured Affordance Space: As with smartphone interfaces, AI can fracture the user's affordance space into disconnected fields, ultimately leading to alienation rather than offering opportunities for mutually informing and enriching cognitive and bodily skills.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In the market research industry, preserving embodiment is critical for: - Developing empathy through face-to-face interaction with research participants - Building trust through embodied presence in client relationships - Interpreting non-verbal cues in qualitative research - Creating meaningful shared experiences that deepen understanding of human behaviors

Organizations should evaluate AI implementations based on whether they preserve or undermine opportunities for embodied capacity development, as outlined in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Entry level squeeze
docs.text: The entry-level squeeze describes the growing pressure on traditional entry-level positions in knowledge work as AI capabilities automate foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds for developing professional expertise.

docs.title: Capacity Development Challenges for Entry-Level Workers
docs.text: While recent evidence shows entry-level headcount is growing among high-intensity AI adopters, the nature of entry-level work is changing in ways that may affect capacity development for junior professionals.

docs.title: Deskilling Risks in Entry-Level Roles
docs.text:
The ai-deskilling-structural-problem framework reveals several risks for entry-level workers:

  • Reduced habituation opportunities: When AI automates routine tasks, entry-level workers lose "the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025)
  • Shallow skill development: Entry into professions may become more superficial without proper mentoring
  • Disembodied learning: Digital workflows may limit embodied interaction necessary for social capacity development
  • Affordance shrinkage: Systematic reduction in action possibilities for developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Structural Dimensions
docs.text:
These challenges are not merely individual responsibility issues but stem from structural conditions:

"We develop and exercise our epistemic, moral, social, and creative capacities in response to our social and material environment" (Ferdman 2026). When entry-level environments become [[capacity-hostile]], junior professionals may struggle to develop the "arts of personhood" required for long-term success.

docs.title: Evidence from Research
docs.text: Studies show that young people growing up with digital tools already struggle with "everyday but essential" skills like empathy, time management, speaking to others, problem-solving and critical thinking (Halliday 2025). AI tools like artificial-personal-assistants could potentially exacerbate this deskilling.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these findings suggest:

  • Entry-level training programs must intentionally preserve opportunities for capacity development
  • Mentorship relationships are crucial for counteracting AI-mediated deskilling
  • Workflows should balance AI augmentation with human skill development
  • Organizations should design capacity-conducive environments for junior staff

The structural perspective emphasizes that "we cannot expect agents to be what Mitcham (2024) calls 'virtuous superheroes' and properly cultivate their human capacities if their social environment does not value the full maturation of these capacities."

See capacity-conducive-environments and habituation-process for related frameworks addressing these challenges.

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-18 Last Updated: 2026-07-19

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis), which are essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions. These capacities are constitutive of human flourishing rather than merely instrumental.

docs.title: Philosophical Framework
docs.text: Based on Ferdman's (2026) analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, epistemic capacities include:

docs.title: Theoretical Rationality
docs.text:
• Thinking and considering reasons to believe
  • Forming accurate beliefs about the world
  • Contemplating complex ideas and concepts
  • Engaging in critical analysis and evaluation

docs.title: Practical Rationality (Phronesis)
docs.text:
• Doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason
  • Knowing effective means to one's ends
  • Possessing accurate understanding of one's situation and circumstances
  • Having discernment: correct understanding of how the good and bad apply in particular circumstances

As Ferdman explains: "To be well motivated is not enough, to have practical wisdom is to be an effective and savvy agent in the real world, equipped with valuable life experience."

docs.title: Role in Life-Planning
docs.text: Epistemic capacities are essential for life-planning because: - They enable self-deliberation on values and goals (theoretical rationality) - They support coordination of goals and intentions with actions (practical wisdom) - They allow for critical reflection on conceptions of a flourishing life - They help set appropriate goals and strive to accomplish them in the right way

docs.title: AI Threats to Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
AI systems threaten epistemic capacities through:

  1. Erosion of critical thinking: "There is growing evidence of the erosion of critical thinking... as a result of overreliance on artificial intelligence" (Bonicalzi et al. 2023; Gerlich 2025; Lee et al. 2025)

  2. Automation bias: In healthcare, AI dependence has been found to diminish diagnostic reasoning and declining clinical judgment (NHS England 2023)

  3. Deskilling of practical wisdom: When AI systems make recommendations, users may outsource the settling and coordination functions of planning, reducing opportunities to develop practical wisdom

  4. Reduced opportunity for self-correction: When plans fail, users may shift responsibility to the AI rather than engaging in self-criticism and improvement

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
Epistemic capacities are fundamental to market research work:

  • Theoretical rationality is required for interpreting complex data and forming accurate insights
  • Practical wisdom is essential for designing appropriate research methodologies and interpreting findings in context
  • Critical thinking enables researchers to evaluate AI-generated insights rather than accepting them uncritically

The increasing use of AI in research threatens these capacities through: - Overreliance on AI-generated summaries and insights - Reduced opportunities for researchers to practice interpretation skills - Narrowing of the field of affordances for developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
To maintain epistemic capacities in AI-augmented research environments: - Preserve space for human interpretation alongside AI analysis - Create structured opportunities for researchers to exercise practical wisdom - Maintain embodied mentorship relationships that support intersubjective habituation - Design workflows that require researchers to explain and justify AI-generated insights

As Ferdman (2026) warns: "Overreliance on APAs could lead to a reduced sense of personal competence... undermining the habituation of the capacities necessary for trusting one's decisions on life-planning." The same principle applies to research decision-making.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The gradual process of becoming skilled through practice, involving inculcation through continued attunement to demands of individual cases, with critical implications for AI's impact on skill development. Skill development cannot be learned through testimony alone but requires practice, encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Process Characteristics
docs.text: According to Ferdman (2026), habituation: - Is a slow, gradual process that cannot be compressed - Requires concrete experience rather than abstract principles - Involves refinement through successive trials and learning from mistakes - Includes encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure - Progresses through stages from novice to expert (Dreyfus and Dreyfus 1986)

docs.title: Intersubjective Dimension
docs.text:
Habituation has two critical components: 1. Intersubjectivity: Requires mentorship where: - Mentor guides novice into proper practice forms - Mentor instills not just mechanical aspects but value of the skill - Shared intentions develop between mentor and mentee - Shared valuing of both skill output and skill itself emerges

  1. Embodiment: Requires physical presence for:
  2. Recognizing others as moral agents through voice and gaze
  3. Creating shared history and participatory sense-making
  4. Developing embodied understanding of social interactions

docs.title: AI's Impact on Habituation
docs.text:
AI systems risk undermining habituation by: - Automating routine tasks that provide necessary practice opportunities - Creating environments where users respond to AI outputs rather than initiating activities - Reducing embodied, intersubjective interactions necessary for shared valuing - Narrowing affordance fields through constant availability and helpful design

Ferdman notes: "Automating routine tasks and leaving only exception-handling to the human user... deprives the user of the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature, leaving them atrophied and unprepared when exceptions arise."

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
In market research, habituation is critical for developing: - epistemic-capacities through repeated data interpretation - social-capacities through client interactions - creative-capacities through research design iterations - volitional-capacity through overcoming research challenges

AI tools that automate foundational research tasks risk creating an entry-level-squeeze by removing the training ground for developing professional expertise through habituation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Human capacities are core abilities that constitute human flourishing, including epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities, which are fundamental to being human and can be undermined by AI systems as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Categories of Human Capacities
docs.text: According to Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, human capacities can be categorized as follows:

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text: The human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding: - Theoretical Rationality: Thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating - Practical Rationality (Phronesis): Doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason; practical wisdom in decision-making

docs.title: Social Capacities
docs.text: The human capacities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life: - Moral Capacity: Recognizing others as moral agents, making ethical judgments - Relational Capacity: Forming meaningful relationships of friendship and love

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text: The human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces: - Involves creating without relying merely on luck, accidents, or mechanical procedures - Enables innovation and adaptation to novel situations

docs.title: Volitional Capacity
docs.text: The human capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow in order to achieve intrinsically valuable goals: - Treated as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities - Required for the difficult process of cultivating other human capacities

docs.title: Why Capacities Matter
docs.text:
Human capacities are fundamental to flourishing for several reasons:

  1. Constitutive Relationship: "The competent exercise of the human capacities is the manifestation of the achievement of the intrinsically valuable goods, making the capacities intrinsically valuable too."

  2. Value of Process: The value of achievements is gained from the competent exercise of capacities involved, not merely from the outcome (e.g., the value of climbing Mt. Everest comes from the climb itself).

  3. Holistic Nature: "Human capacities rarely operate in isolation from each other... capacity-hostile environments are typically hostile to the capacities in that they undermine the opportunity to engage in activities that involve the exercise a combination of the capacities at a time."

docs.title: Capacity-Deskilling vs. Skill Obsolescence
docs.text:
It's important to distinguish between innocuous skill obsolescence and harmful capacity-deskilling:

  • Skill Obsolescence: "Skill obsolescence has always been part of human history, where technological developments free up time and resources for the cultivation of other skills." Deskilling of activities like hunting or basket-weaving may be innocuous.

  • Capacity-Deskilling: "The deskilling of our core human capacities—to know, create, form meaningful relationships, and use our willpower—is a different matter." Capacity-deskilling should always be a cause for worry because inadequate development of these capacities diminishes us as humans.

docs.title: Impact of AI on Human Capacities
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine human capacities through several mechanisms:

  1. Capacity-Hostile Environments: AI can create environments that restrict opportunities for capacity development and exercise.

  2. Automation Bias: Offloading tasks to AI can lead to erosion of critical thinking, decision-making, and analytical reasoning.

  3. Disembodied Interaction: Digital interfaces limit opportunities for embodied interaction necessary for social and moral capacities.

  4. Plan-Following Orientation: AI tools that encourage users to follow pre-determined plans rather than form their own undermine practical rationality.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In the market research industry, preserving human capacities is critical for: - Developing epistemic capacities for interpreting complex human behaviors - Exercising social capacities to build trust with research participants - Applying creative capacities to design innovative research approaches - Using volitional capacity to overcome research challenges and ethical dilemmas

Organizations should evaluate AI implementations based on whether they support or undermine researchers' human capacities, as outlined in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Human operating model gap
docs.text: The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations.

docs.title: Workforce Composition Changes with AI Adoption
docs.text: Recent evidence reveals how AI adoption is reshaping workforce composition across roles, highlighting the growing gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and slower human system adaptation.

docs.title: Role-Specific Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study provides detailed evidence of how AI adoption affects different job functions:

  • Broad-based growth: High-intensity adopters showed growth across multiple roles:
  • Sales headcount: +10.3%
  • Administrative headcount: +7.8%
  • Engineering headcount: +7.3%
  • Customer service headcount: +6.3%

  • Scientist headcount: +5.6%

  • Entry-level expansion: Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% among high-intensity adopters

  • Managerial shifts: Manager-plus share fell by 1.52 percentage points despite overall growth

docs.title: Structural Workforce Shifts
docs.text:
These findings reveal several important patterns:

  1. Non-binary impact: AI adoption doesn't simply eliminate jobs but reshapes workforce composition
  2. Intensity matters: Only high-intensity adopters (top tercile of AI spend) showed significant growth
  3. Gradual emergence: Gains followed a learning curve, emerging 6-12 months after adoption
  4. Sector concentration: Effects were strongest in the Information sector

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these workforce shifts suggest:

  • AI is currently augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities in information work
  • Strategic AI investment may support growth across multiple functions
  • Entry-level positions may expand as firms scale with AI assistance
  • Workforce planning must account for the gradual nature of AI integration

The study notes that "the earliest signs of growth emerge roughly 6-12 months after adoption, perhaps after firms establish best practices, integrate AI tools into workflows, and are subsequently able to make new investments and hire staff."

docs.title: Bridging the Gap
docs.text:
To address the human operating model gap, market research firms should:

  • Develop AI adoption strategies that align with workforce development
  • Create pathways for employees to develop AI-augmented capabilities
  • Recognize that successful integration requires time for habituation
  • Design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for skill development

See value-chain-shift and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational structures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Intersubjectivity in skilling refers to the shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide and share the value of the skill. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to instill not only the mechanical aspects but also the value of the skill, with critical implications for AI's impact on capacity development.

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, intersubjectivity in skilling has several critical features:

  1. Mentor-Guided Development: Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to guide the novice into becoming an expert that engages in practice of the right kind.

  2. Shared Valuing: A good mentor instills not only the mechanical aspects of the skill but, as importantly, the value of the skill, such that the skilled agent eventually comes to view the value of the skill as their own.

  3. Shared Intentions: In the mentor-mentee relationship, both parties have shared intentions and come to have "shared valuing" of the skill.

  4. Societal Dimension: Skill habituation occurs not just in individual relationships but also through social practices performed by groups or whole societies.

docs.title: Role in Capacity Development
docs.text:
Intersubjectivity is fundamental to human capacity development:

  1. Value Transmission: Learning to value a capacity is part of the process of its habituation. Without intersubjective transmission of value, persons cannot learn to value more masterful levels of capacities.

  2. Moral Reason Generation: As Kate Manne argues, social practices are often what generates moral reasons for action, as they have a constitutive aim or telos, which is ultimately the aim of helping people fare well rather than badly.

  3. Learning Through Common Life: Alasdair MacIntyre noted that learning is carried out through the practices of the common life: becoming the kind of agent who is responsive to skillful action "has to be learned from teachers and exemplars who know how to communicate this kind of responsiveness to others through the habits of a common life."

  4. Shared Understanding of Outputs: Social practices play an important role in the formation of shared valuing regarding both the outputs (the product of the skilled activity) and the skill itself.

docs.title: Impact of AI on Intersubjectivity
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine intersubjectivity in several ways:

  1. Reduced Human Interaction: As AI mediation replaces more human activity, it decreases opportunities for developing capacities in concert with other humans.

  2. Diminished Shared Valuing: When AI tools replace human mentors, they cannot transmit the shared valuing of skills that is essential for deep capacity development.

  3. Individualized Learning: AI personalization creates isolated learning experiences rather than shared practices that generate moral reasons for action.

  4. Disembodied Guidance: Even when AI provides mentorship-like functions, the lack of embodiment limits the depth of intersubjective connection necessary for capacity development.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In the market research industry, preserving intersubjectivity is critical for: - Developing shared understanding of research quality standards - Transmitting the value of ethical research practices across generations - Building meaningful client relationships based on shared valuing - Creating mentorship opportunities that develop both technical skills and professional values

Organizations should evaluate AI implementations based on whether they preserve or undermine opportunities for intersubjective capacity development, as outlined in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. As demonstrated by the contrast between exposure-based studies and spending-based research like the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, methodological choices fundamentally shape conclusions about AI's labor market effects.

docs.title: Evidence of Heterogeneity
docs.text:
Study Type Primary Method Key Employment Finding Example Exposure-based Occupational AI exposure scores Negative impact on entry-level jobs Brynjolfsson et al. (2025) Spending-based Observed AI vendor payments Positive impact at high intensity Ramp-Revelio study Survey-based Executive adoption surveys Mixed or positive impacts Yotzov et al. (2026)

The Ramp-Revelio study documents this heterogeneity through direct comparison: - Exposure-based studies predict job losses in high-exposure occupations - Spending-based research shows job growth among high-intensity adopters - The discrepancy stems from methodological differences, not contradictory realities

docs.title: Root Causes
docs.text: Three fundamental methodological differences drive these divergent findings:

docs.title: 1. Adoption Measurement
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Measure theoretical task feasibility ("could AI do this?")
  • Spending data: Measure actual adoption behavior ("is the firm paying for AI?")
  • Surveys: Capture self-reported usage ("do executives say they use AI?")

As the Ramp-Revelio study notes: "These estimates are closer to the Ramp–Revelio paid-adoption series than the firm-weighted BTOS benchmark, but they still measure a different object."

docs.title: 2. Intensity Dimension
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Typically binary or quintile-based
  • Spending data: Reveals continuous intensity effects (PEPM metric)
  • Surveys: Often lack precise intensity measures

The Ramp-Revelio study found only high-intensity adopters showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no change.

docs.title: 3. Selection Bias Handling
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Cannot distinguish adopters from non-adopters with identical workforce
  • Spending data: Enables direct comparison of adopters vs. later adopters
  • Surveys: Often lack pre-adoption data for comparison

The Ramp-Revelio study documents substantial pre-adoption differences that confound simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological heterogeneity creates critical challenges:

  • Conflicting guidance: Different studies recommend opposite actions based on methodology
  • Implementation uncertainty: Hard to predict AI impact without knowing intensity threshold
  • Evaluation complexity: Must select appropriate methodology for specific context
  • Vendor claims: AI providers may cite favorable methodology while ignoring others

docs.title: Strategic Response Framework
docs.text:
Market research organizations should adopt a methodologically sophisticated approach:

  1. Triangulate findings: Consider evidence from multiple methodological approaches
  2. Assess intensity: Focus on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact
  3. Control for selection: Account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI
  4. Contextualize results: Recognize sector-specific effects (e.g., concentrated in Information)

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept explains the contradictory findings between the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study (showing 12.0% entry-level growth) and exposure-based studies predicting job losses. It represents the methodological foundation for understanding the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and the value of the ai-adoption-methodological-innovation in spending-based measurement.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, navigating methodological heterogeneity requires: - Never relying on a single study's methodology for decision-making - Understanding the measurement approach behind any AI impact claim - Recognizing that "AI adoption" has no single empirical rate (as shown in Ramp-Revelio Figure 1) - Focusing on high-intensity implementation thresholds rather than binary adoption

Without this methodological sophistication, organizations risk making decisions based on incomplete or misleading evidence about AI's true impact.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A narrow field of affordances is an environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities, a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile environments as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, narrow fields of affordances have several critical features:

  1. Limited Action Possibilities: The environment offers fewer opportunities for engaging in activities that trigger human capacities.

  2. Systematic Restriction: The limitation is not random but systematically restricts certain types of capacities, particularly epistemic, social, moral, and creative capacities.

  3. Discouraged Compensation: The environment not only restricts opportunities but also discourages users from seeking alternative avenues to compensate for the shrinkage.

  4. Cumulative Effect: Narrow fields of affordances become particularly problematic when multiple human activities are automated across multiple spheres (writing, searching, planning, organizing, navigation, decision-making).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Healthcare AI Systems: Afford the possibility of offloading tasks to the machine, leading to automation bias where users attribute excessive trust to AI tools, risking the loss of critical skills necessary for unexpected scenarios.

  2. Smartphone Interfaces: Provide possibilities for interaction that are disconnected from other persons (swiping, clicking, scrolling), fracturing the user's affordance space into disconnected fields, ultimately leading to alienation.

  3. Artificial Personal Assistants: Constantly available and designed to be helpful, they discourage users from seeking out new opportunities for growth and exploration by replacing most planning activities.

  4. Social Media Platforms: Create environments that herd users to behave in certain ways through targeted ads and filtered newsfeeds, restricting opportunities for critical thinking and meaningful social interaction.

docs.title: Impact on Capacity Development
docs.text:
Narrow fields of affordances undermine human capacity development in several ways:

  1. Shallow Skilling: They afford only superficial development of capacities without opportunities for mastery.

  2. Capacity Atrophy: When persons develop capacities in shallow ways, they cannot learn to value more masterful levels of those capacities, leading to capacity atrophy.

  3. Reduced Habituation: They deprive users of the routine opportunities to practice judgment and strengthen their "cognitive musculature," leaving them unprepared when exceptions arise.

  4. Automation Bias: They encourage offloading tasks to machines, creating environments where users attribute authority or excessive trust to AI tools over advice from other sources.

docs.title: Affordance Shrinkage
docs.text:
Narrow fields of affordances become normatively problematic when they lead to "affordance shrinkage" - when the reduction in action possibilities is systematic, enduring, and deeply entrenched, such that it discourages users from finding ways to compensate for the shrinkage. This is particularly concerning with AI because:

  1. Cumulative Automation: "Automation and replacement of human activity is becoming more prevalent, across many human spheres."

  2. Discouraged Compensation: "The more the APA does things for the user, the more it could constitute a capacity-hostile environment... discouraging the user from seeking out new opportunities for growth and exploration."

  3. Structural Nature: The problem is structural rather than individual - "the context in which a user's behavior occurs can better explain the behavior than appealing to the user's dispositions."

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In the market research industry, narrow fields of affordances could undermine researchers' abilities to: - Exercise critical thinking when interpreting complex data - Develop creative approaches to research design - Build meaningful client relationships through embodied interaction - Exercise moral judgment in ethical research practices

Organizations should evaluate AI implementations based on whether they create narrow or rich fields of affordances for researchers' capacity development, as outlined in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) is a metric developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to measure the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level. It calculates monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained AI adoption begins.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
PEPM = (Σ²ₘ₌₀ AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ) / (3 × HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁)

Where: - AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ = AI vendor spend for firm i in month m after adoption - HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁ = baseline headcount in the month before adoption

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. AI adoption is defined as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  2. PEPM is calculated using AI spend over the first three months after adoption begins
  3. Baseline headcount is measured in the month before adoption
  4. Firms are sorted into intensity groups:
  5. High intensity: top PEPM tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom two PEPM terciles

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
• Provides a direct, observed measure of AI adoption intensity rather than relying on occupational exposure scores
  • Allows researchers to distinguish between firms that adopt AI lightly versus intensively
  • Correlates closely with adoption of more complex AI products and tools (coding agents, APIs) versus simpler chat subscriptions
  • Enables analysis of differential impacts based on adoption intensity

docs.title: Key Findings Using PEPM
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters (top tercile) grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Gains emerged gradually, suggesting a "learning curve" as firms integrated AI tools

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The plan-forming vs plan-following distinction refers to the critical difference between actively creating plans through self-deliberation (requiring agential control) versus executing pre-determined plans (more habitual), with critical implications for AI's impact on capacity development as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text: According to Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this distinction has several critical features:

docs.title: Plan-Forming
docs.text:
1. Agential Control: Requires exercising control over initiating the activity of forming a plan.
  2. Self-Deliberation: Involves thoughtful consideration of values, goals, and circumstances.
  3. Two Key Functions:
  4. Settling Function: Managing finite cognitive resources when facing choices between options
  5. Coordination Function: Forming and organizing different types of plans and future-directed intentions
  6. Responsibility Taking: Involves taking responsibility if the plan fails, affording opportunities for self-criticism and improvement
  7. Practical Wisdom: Requires practical rationality (phronesis) - doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason

docs.title: Plan-Following
docs.text:
1. Environmental Trigger Response: Initiated in response to triggers in the environment rather than self-initiated
  2. Habitual Execution: More like a habit that is developed in response to environmental triggers
  3. Limited Agential Control: Lacks control over initiating the planning activity
  4. Reduced Responsibility: When plans fail, responsibility can be shifted to the plan creator (e.g., an AI system)
  5. Shallow Skill Development: Affords only superficial development of capacities without opportunities for mastery

docs.title: Role in Capacity Development
docs.text:
This distinction is fundamental to human capacity development:

  1. Epistemic Capacities: Plan-forming requires theoretical rationality (thinking, considering reasons to believe) and practical rationality (phronesis).

  2. Social Capacities: Planning involves coordinating with others toward achieving complex goals, drawing on social relationships for life goals.

  3. Creative Capacities: Plan-forming requires the ability to reconsider and respond to novel situations, surprises, and unexpected events.

  4. Volitional Capacity: Plan-forming requires developing and exercising the capacity to will oneself into initiating the activity of forming a plan.

docs.title: Impact of AI on Plan-Forming
docs.text:
AI systems, particularly Artificial Personal Assistants, can undermine plan-forming in several ways:

  1. APA Integration: APAs afford the replacement of many activities involved in both planning and executing plans, which would otherwise require proper cultivation of epistemic, social, moral, and creative capacities.

  2. Trigger-Based Responses: Users begin by asking the APA for help forming plans, then follow the APA's recommendations, responding to the APA's output as an environmental trigger rather than initiating planning themselves.

  3. Reduced Practical Wisdom: "Overreliance on APAs could lead to a reduced sense of personal competence... undermining the habituation of the capacities necessary for trusting one's decisions on life-planning."

  4. Responsibility Shifting: "If an APA makes a plan that ends up failing, the user could more readily shift the responsibility to the APA, forgoing the opportunity for self-growth."

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In the market research industry, preserving plan-forming capabilities is critical for: - Developing research strategies through self-deliberation rather than following formulaic approaches - Exercising practical wisdom in research design and interpretation - Taking responsibility for research outcomes and ethical considerations - Creating innovative research approaches that respond to novel situations

Organizations should evaluate AI implementations based on whether they encourage plan-forming or promote plan-following behaviors among researchers, as outlined in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.
